final_answer:
Special relativity establishes that the speed of light (c) is an invariant, the same for all observers regardless of their motion. This stems from two postulates: (1) physical laws are identical in all inertial frames, and (2) the speed of light in vacuum is constant. 

If an object had a speed v > c, the Lorentz factor gamma (γ = 1/√(1 - v²/c²)) would become imaginary, violating physical reality. As v approaches c, γ diverges to infinity, implying energy and momentum (p = γmv) would require infinite input to accelerate further. Since infinite energy is unattainable, no object with mass can reach or exceed c. 

Velocity addition in relativity also ensures that combining speeds near c still yields results ≤ c, preserving causality. Exceeding c would allow signals to propagate backward in time, creating paradoxes. Thus, c is the cosmic speed limit, enforced by spacetime’s structure.
